caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:hc-21
attempts.entry_title: Space in the macaque hippocampus during virtual navigation (Wirth et al. 2017)
attempts.summary: Some central findings on hippocampal cells of monkeys navigating a virtual maze held up in this data, several did not, and those involving gaze could not be tested. Maps in the task's state space carried more information than position and direction maps and were sparser than direction maps. Fewer cells were significant in state space (57 against the paper's 84), fewer coded distance to landmarks, and selectivity for the rotation at the maze centre failed under an assumed surrogate method the paper leaves open. Gaze maps, foveation-aligned responses and the direction tuning comparisons need a calibrated eye signal, which the files lack. Of the minor claims, gaze anticipation and learning speed reproduced and probe-session transfer did not.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Wirth, Baraduc, Plante, Pinede and Duhamel (2017) on CRCNS hc-12, which holds 189 hippocampal cells of two macaques navigating a virtual star maze with eye tracking, and uses CRCNS hc-21 to check which of its recordings are also in hc-12. It covers learning, gaze before turns and on passive returns, information content in position, direction and state space, centre and return direction maps, state-space selectivity and the landmark ANOVAs. The point-of-gaze analyses need a calibration of the eye signal that the files do not give.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Wirth et al. (2017) from CRCNS hc-12

outcomes.statement: During the 500 ms before each joystick action, gaze anticipated the direction of the subsequent movement.
outcomes.source: Results, Animals use direction and compute trajectory, paragraph 2; S1 Fig and S2 Fig (S2A and S2B legend)
outcomes.quote: During the 500 ms before each action on the joystick ( Fig 1D , S1 Fig , S2 Fig , and S1 Appendix A2), gaze anticipated the direction of the subsequent movement (Wilcoxon test, p < 0.001
outcomes.notes: Before right turns (code 1) the horizontal eye signal, standardized within session, lies on the negative side of that before left turns (code 2) in each monkey, in the 500 and the 300 ms windows, for each eye and both eyes, successful or all trials, with rank-sum p below 1e-100. 500 ms, both eyes, successful trials, K median difference -0.77 session SD (p = 4.0e-148, 39 of 40 sessions, signed-rank across sessions p = 1.3e-11), S -1.00 (p = 4.3e-146, 20 of 20 sessions, p = 1.9e-6). Negative is rightward by the slow phases (deviations), so gaze lies on the side of the coming turn. Both monkeys, each window and the pooled test agree, so the readings of the criterion give one outcome. In the 500 ms before the code the view already rotates slowly toward the turn (median 0.49 to 0.75 degrees, in that direction in 95% to 99% of turns), and in K the eye velocity there differs between right and left turns in the direction of the slow phases (0.250 against -0.189 session SD, 38 of 40 sessions, p = 2.3e-9); in S it does not (9 of 20, p = 0.40). The position effect remains in turns with less than 0.25 degrees of rotation before the code (K -0.27 session SD, p = 3.3e-5; S -0.54, p = 0.0059) and less than 1 degree (K -0.37, S -0.695), where K's velocity difference also remains (0.248, p = 2.6e-10). Part of K's position effect may continue an eye movement under way before the window; it is a third to a half as large in the low-rotation turns as over all turns. The S2B control (second of two turns) was not run.
deviations: The eye signal has no calibration, units or sign in the files, and is on a +-5000 scale in 36 sessions and a +-5 scale in 26. Values are standardized within each session (minus the session median, over its SD) before sessions are pooled; per-session differences are also counted and tested across sessions.

Assumed that a negative horizontal value is rightward, from the slow phases. During a turn the scene flows across the screen opposite to the turn and the slow phases of optokinetic nystagmus and pursuit follow it; the median eye velocity from 0 to 600 ms after the code is positive during right turns and negative during left turns in 40 of 40 sessions of K and 20 of 20 of S (signed-rank p = 1.8e-12 and 1.9e-6). This uses the eye velocity only, not the position the claim tests. The mean position during the turn moves toward the turn, as it does during optokinetic stimulation.
S1 Appendix A2, which holds the paper's analysis, was not available; the test is the rank-sum of the claims file.

outcomes.statement: When relocated to a new entry, the monkeys gazed proactively at the location where the landmarks would appear.
outcomes.source: Results, Animals use direction and compute trajectory, paragraph 2; S2C Fig
outcomes.quote: Similarly, when being relocated to a new entry, monkeys proactively gazed at the location at which the landmarks would appear (see S2 Fig and S1 Appendix A2) (Wilcoxon test, p < 0.001)
outcomes.notes: Passive returns (tags 5xy) turn right when the camera orientation falls over them, as it does after code 1. During right-turning returns the standardized eye signal lies on the negative (rightward) side in each monkey (all returns, both eyes, K -0.56 session SD, p = 6.2e-58, 39 of 41 sessions, signed-rank across sessions p = 1.3e-9; S -0.56, p = 6.4e-30, 20 of 21 sessions, p = 1.9e-6) and after successful trials only (p = 4.7e-34 and 1.5e-10). The sign is set by the slow phases during turns at the centre, which do not use eye position; the eye velocity over the returns gives the same sign (40 of 41 and 21 of 21 sessions). The test measures where the eyes are during the return, as the criterion does; whether this is anticipation or the eye position that goes with any rotation of the view cannot be told apart here. The criterion, which takes the mean over the whole return, does not test the proactive part of the claim; this is asked of a reader in questions/wirth-2017.yaml, and the claim is tested as the claims file has it.
deviations: The same standardization and sign as gaze-anticipates-action.
The side of a return is taken from the change of camera orientation over it (median absolute change 102.5 degrees); the files do not say where the landmarks appear.

outcomes.statement: Both monkeys learned the rewarded arm in about a dozen trials; monkey S performed above chance after 12.3 plus or minus 2 trials (SEM) and monkey K after 14.8 plus or minus 2.4.
outcomes.source: Results, Animals use direction and compute trajectory, paragraph 3; S3A and S3B Fig
outcomes.quote: monkey S performed above chance after 12.3 ± 2 trials (SEM), and monkey K did so after 14.8 ± 2.4 trials
outcomes.notes: Using the files' own learning curves, the first trial whose lower bound exceeds 1/4 is on average 12.26 +- 3.28 (SEM, 23 sessions) for monkey S and 16.53 +- 2.69 (38 sessions) for monkey K over all sessions (reading a), and 15.82 +- 3.44 for K without the probe sessions (reading b). Both monkeys fall within the paper's SEMs under both readings. Two sessions of S and three of K never reach the criterion and are left out. The field learningtrial of every session equals this trial.
deviations: The curves are the files' own; the method of the paper's reference 60 is not named in the text read. The columns are read as probability, lower and upper bound, as the values show, where the descriptor puts the probability in the middle column.

outcomes.statement: From above-chance performance to the upper confidence bound of success reaching 90%, fewer than 10 trials were usually needed (89% of sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, Animals use direction and compute trajectory, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: From then to when the upper confidence bound of success reached 90%, less than 10 trials were usually necessary (89% of sessions).
outcomes.notes: Of the 59 sessions that reach both the lower bound above 1/4 and the upper bound at 0.9, 53 need fewer than 10 trials between them (0.898). Over all 66 sessions the fraction is 0.803, also within 0.89 +- 0.089, and without the probe sessions 0.898 and 0.815. One session has its upper bound at 0.9 already at the criterion trial (0 trials); the median is 2 trials and the upper bound at the criterion trial has a median of 0.835. Without that session the fraction is 52 of 58 (0.897).
deviations: The denominator is not stated; the fraction is given over the sessions reaching both criteria and over all sessions, and both match.

outcomes.statement: In probe sessions, performance after the new western entries were introduced was higher than at the start of the session (monkey K 73% against 44%, monkey S 80% against 55%).
outcomes.source: Results, Animals use direction and compute trajectory, paragraph 4; S3C Fig and legend
outcomes.quote: Monkey K was 73% correct after introducing the new entries versus 44% correct at beginning of the sessions; monkey S was 80% versus 55% correct ( S3C Fig , Wilcoxon, p = 0.01).

statistics.n: 9 probe sessions for monkey S and 15 for monkey K

outcomes.notes: hc-12 holds 12 probe sessions of monkey K (the paper reports 15) and none of monkey S (the paper reports 9); the 8 probe-like sessions of hc-21 are among the 12. For K, 28.3% correct over the first 5 trials and 58.3% over the 5 trials after the new entries, both below the paper's 44% and 73% by more than the tolerance; Wilcoxon signed-rank over the 12 sessions p = 0.072 (median gain 0.30). The first entries lie on one side of the rewarded arm in 9 sessions (clockwise in 2, counterclockwise in 7) and on both sides in 3, where the paper describes northeastern and southeastern entries. No variant brings both means within tolerance: the first 5 trials from a new entry give 60.0% (p = 0.057); the 9 one-sided sessions give 15.6% and 62.2% (p = 0.023); the 5 sessions whose introduction comes after trial 20 give 16.0% and 64.0% (p = 0.125). The two values of monkey S could not be computed; the criterion fails on K's values alone.
deviations: Probe sessions are found from the start arms (the first 10 trials use one or two entries and later ones others), as the files do not mark them. The introduction is the first trial from an entry not used in the first 10 (S3C legend); the variants are shown.
The measured values are monkey K's, after and at the start; monkey S has no probe session in the data.

outcomes.statement: In probe sessions, performance above the learning criterion was reached faster after the new entries (within 4 trials for monkey K and 2.7 for monkey S, against 14.8 and 12.3).
outcomes.source: Results, Animals use direction and compute trajectory, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Further, performances above the learning criterion were reached significantly faster (within 4 trials for monkey K and within 2.7 trials for monkey S, compared to 14.8 and 12.3 trials; Wilcoxon, p = 0.002).
outcomes.notes: Counting trials to criterion from the introduction of the new entries needs learning curves recomputed on part of the session, with the confidence bounds of the paper's reference 60, which the text read does not name (S3B legend, "methods based on [60]"). The files hold only whole-session curves. Any other curve method would set the criterion differently. hc-12 also holds no probe session of monkey S. The question is for the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: Of 270 cells recorded in the right hippocampus (128 in monkey S, 142 in monkey K), 189 fired more than 100 spikes per session and were analysed.
outcomes.source: Results, What is encoded in hippocampal cell activity, paragraph 1; Methods, Electrophysiological recordings
outcomes.quote: Of the 270 cells recorded in the full extent of the right hippocampus (128 cells in monkey S, 142 in monkey K; S4 Fig ), we focused on 189 cells that fired more than 100 spikes per session
outcomes.notes: hc-12 holds 189 cell files (99 of monkey K, 90 of monkey S), the paper's analysed count; 187 have new-maze data and 186 fire more than 100 spikes in the new-maze session (within 189 +- 18.9). The 270 cells recorded (128 S, 142 K) are not deposited beyond these 189, so that count cannot be checked. The files give recording coordinates but no subfield.

outcomes.statement: 111 of the 189 cells (59%) had significant information content in at least one of the four coding spaces.
outcomes.source: Results, Sensitivity of the cells to a combination of variables, paragraph 2; Fig 3A
outcomes.quote: Significant IC ( p < 0.01) was present in at least one of the spaces for 111 out of the 189 cells (59%, responsive cells).
outcomes.notes: Responsiveness is defined over four spaces, one of them the point of gaze, which needs the gaze direction in degrees; the eye signal has no calibration, units or sign in the files. Responsive in the three spaces computed here are 59 of 186 cells (full trials, permuted chunks; 51, 55, 47, 59 and 52 under the other readings), a lower bound of the four-space count, which could lie anywhere from 59 to 186.

outcomes.statement: The proportions of cells responsive to each space were unequal; the state space accounted for the most cells (84), and more cells were responsive to state space than to point of gaze.
outcomes.source: Results, Sensitivity of the cells to a combination of variables, paragraph 2; Fig 3A
outcomes.quote: The proportion of cells responsive to each space was significantly unequal (chi-squared test, p = 0.014). The state space accounted for the largest number (84 cells, Fig 3A ), and pitting state space against the other three, there were more cells responsive to state space than to point of gaze (chi-squared test, p = 0.012, Bonferroni corrected

statistics.about: state space against point of gaze

outcomes.notes: 57 of 186 cells have significant state-space IC under the main reading (full trials, permuted chunks) and 47, 42, 37, 57 and 47 under the other five readings (shifted chunks; start to reward; start to reward with the returns), all below 75.6 to 92.4. With the upper tail alone the counts are 41 to 58. The count needs no gaze, so the missing gaze space does not change the outcome; the chi-squared tests across the four spaces could not be run. State space has the most cells of the three spaces computed under every reading (57 against 46 for position and 40 for direction under the main reading).
deviations: Map resolution steps (square bins for position and state space, as in the dataset's scripts, equal angular bins for direction), two readings of the surrogate shifting and three of the trial window, as in the claims file (Method W). The start to reward window with the returns is almost the full one, as the trial ends at the reward (median 0 s from code 11 to 23).

The shift reading rotates each 5 s chunk within itself by its own random offset. The first version moved each chunk over the whole session, so chunks overlapped; on synthetic trains without coding its surrogates had 2.1 times the actual IC and every train came out significant. The corrected version gives 3.3% of such trains p < 0.01 (permuted chunks 0%).

outcomes.statement: Sensitivity to the four variables was not mutually exclusive; most responsive cells carried significant activity in more than one coding space.
outcomes.source: Results, Sensitivity of the cells to a combination of variables, paragraph 2; Fig 3B legend
outcomes.quote: Most responsive cells carry significant activity in more than one coding space.
outcomes.notes: Depends on responsive-cells (the gaze space). Of the 59 cells responsive in the three spaces computed, 46 are significant in two or more; cells responsive only in gaze space would add to the denominator, so the fraction over the paper's set cannot be bounded above one half.

outcomes.statement: For direction-selective cells, both information per spike and sparsity of directional firing were higher in the maze center than on the peripheral return paths.
outcomes.source: Results, Direction selectivity, paragraph 1; Fig 3C
outcomes.quote: Both IC and sparsity measures were significantly higher in the center, which is the choice point, when compared to return tracks (both p < 0.001).
outcomes.notes: For the 40 cells with significant direction IC (reading a, permuted chunks) normalized sparsity is higher in the centre than on return paths (median difference 0.020, 25 of 40, Wilcoxon p = 0.031) and IC is not (0.012, p = 0.43); with shifted chunks (28 cells) p = 0.016 and 0.095. Reading (a) meets neither level. Reading (b) needs the paper's responsive set, which needs the point-of-gaze space. Over the 59 three-space responsive cells, which it contains, IC and sparsity are both higher with p = 0.045 and 0.0074, the partial level; with shifted chunks (51 cells) IC is not (p = 0.14, sparsity p = 0.013). Over all 180 cells with both maps neither is higher (IC p = 0.31, sparsity p = 0.29, permuted chunks), so a signed-rank result over the 59 cells puts no bound on the result over the paper's set, which may lie at any level. No set reaches p < 0.001. Reading (a) fails and reading (b) cannot be formed, so the claim cannot be decided, as for landmark-identity-center.
deviations: Centre and return maps at one common angular resolution per session, chosen so the number of bins valid in both is closest to 200 (median 151 centre and 157.5 return bins valid); the paper does not say how the two maps were binned.
Reading (b), all responsive cells, cannot be formed without the gaze space; the three-space responsive cells, which it contains, stand in for it, an assumption.

outcomes.statement: Direction tuning was not maintained across positions; the correlation between directional tuning in the center and on return paths was significantly low in 20 of 56 cells (36%), more than chance, and significantly high in only 3, consistent with chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Direction selectivity, paragraph 1; Fig 3C inset
outcomes.quote: the correlation between direction selectivity in the center and in the return paths was significantly lower in 20 out of 56 cells (inset in Fig 3C , blue bars). This represents 36% of the population and is higher than what is expected by chance ( p < 0.001, binomial test; note that correlation was only significantly higher in 3 cells, consistent with chance: p = 0.16, binomial test)
outcomes.notes: Of 40 direction-selective cells (permuted chunks), 15 (38%) have a significantly low centre-return correlation (binomial p = 2.1e-14 at chance 0.025) and 4 a significantly high one (p = 0.017). The high count is inside 2 to 4, but the number of cells tested (40, expected 56 +- 5.6) and the low count (15, expected 20 +- 2) are outside the tolerance. Over the 59 three-space responsive cells 16 are low and 4 high; with shifted chunks 11 of 28 and 14 of 51 are low. Over these sets the low count misses 18 to 22, although more cells than chance have a low correlation under all of them (binomial p below 1e-10). The criterion has no partial level. Reading (a) fails on the number of cells (40 and 28). Reading (b) needs the paper's responsive set, which needs the point-of-gaze space. That set lies between the three-space responsive cells and all cells (181 tested, 25 low and 8 high with permuted chunks; 18 and 7 with shifted chunks), and a set between the two can meet the criterion, in one combination with permuted chunks (n 61, low 18, high 4) and in 13 with shifted chunks (for example n 55, low 18, high 3). A set that meets the criterion and one that fails it (the stand-in) both exist, so the claim cannot be decided.
deviations: Cells with at least 10 common valid bins, a standard choice for "enough"; with 2 the counts do not change.
Reading (b), all responsive cells, cannot be formed without the gaze space; the three-space responsive cells stand in for it, an assumption, as in direction-center-vs-periphery.

outcomes.statement: Spike information content was systematically higher in state space than in position, direction or point-of-gaze space, for cells responsive in both spaces compared.
outcomes.source: Results, Hippocampal cells encode a fine-grained state-space representation, paragraph 1; Fig 3D to 3F
outcomes.quote: The spike information content for the state space was systematically higher when compared to position, direction, or gaze space (Wilcoxon, all p < 0.01).
outcomes.notes: Normalized IC is higher in state space than in position space (full trials, permuted chunks: 44 cells, median difference 0.014, 35 higher, Wilcoxon p = 1.1e-4) and than in direction space (40 cells, 0.021, 35 higher, p = 2.5e-7), with p < 0.01 under all six readings (largest 0.0022). The comparison with the point-of-gaze space cannot be made, as the eye signal has no calibration, so two of the three comparisons hold, the criterion's partial level.
deviations: The cells of each comparison are those significant in both spaces compared, which needs no gaze; the point-of-gaze comparison is missing.

outcomes.statement: Sparsity was significantly higher in state space than in direction space.
outcomes.source: Results, Hippocampal cells encode a fine-grained state-space representation, paragraph 1; Fig 3E
outcomes.quote: Sparsity was significantly higher (Wilcoxon test) in state space compared to direction space ( p = 0.006)
outcomes.notes: For the 40 cells with significant IC in both state and direction space (full trials, permuted chunks), normalized sparsity is higher in state space (median difference 0.016, 28 of 40 cells, Wilcoxon p = 0.0022); with shifted chunks, 27 cells, 0.020, p = 0.0059. With the start-to-reward window it is not significant (p = 0.92 and 0.98); the start-to-reward window with the returns gives the full-trial numbers. The outcome rests on keeping the returns in the maps.
deviations: The main reading takes the trial window from start to next start (the state space includes the returns, Fig 1F legend); the paper does not settle it, and the outcome depends on it (findings). Both surrogate readings agree.

outcomes.statement: Sparsity was not significantly higher in state space than in position space overall, but the 15 cells whose difference was individually significant were sparser in state space.
outcomes.source: Results, Hippocampal cells encode a fine-grained state-space representation, paragraph 1; Fig 3D
outcomes.quote: but not significantly higher compared to position space ( p = 0.19), although the 15 cells for which the difference was individually significant (as assessed with permutation tests on surrogate data) were sparser in state space ( p = 0.001)

statistics.about: all cells responsive in both spaces
the 15 cells with an individually significant difference

outcomes.notes: State space is significantly sparser than position space over the cells responsive in both under every reading (Wilcoxon p = 0.00013 to 0.00043, median difference 0.014 to 0.028; main reading 44 cells, 0.016, p = 0.00043), where the paper's test finds no significant difference. 7 to 11 cells (per-cell level 0.05) or 3 to 5 (0.01) differ individually, against 15 +- 1.5 (main reading 9 and 5); those cells are sparser in state space (p = 0.00098 to 0.016 at level 0.05). No reading meets the first two parts.

outcomes.statement: Sparsity was higher overall in point-of-gaze space than in state space, an effect not confirmed among the 18 cells whose difference was individually significant.
outcomes.source: Results, Hippocampal cells encode a fine-grained state-space representation, paragraph 1; Fig 3F
outcomes.quote: Conversely, sparsity was significantly higher overall in gaze space than in state space ( p < 0.001), but this effect could not be confirmed when considering only 18 cells for which the difference was individually significant ( p = 0.68).

statistics.about: all cells responsive in both spaces
the 18 cells with an individually significant difference

outcomes.notes: Needs the point-of-gaze space; the eye signal has no calibration.

outcomes.statement: In the maze center, at the same position and direction, 12 of 111 responsive cells (11%) showed significantly high state-space selectivity, discriminating the current rotational move, more than chance; only 4 showed significantly low selectivity, as expected by chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Cells discriminate different contexts for the same position and direction, paragraph 1; Fig 4B
outcomes.quote: Only 4 cells showed significantly low state-space selectivity, as expected by chance ( p = 0.81, binomial test), but 12 cells out of 111 (11%, p = 0.01, binomial test) showed significantly high state-space selectivity
outcomes.notes: The paper's responsive set contains the three-space responsive cells and lies within all cells, so its counts are bounded by the counts over these two sets. With permuted chunks the low count over the three-space responsive cells is already 6 or 7 under every move typing and trial window, above the 3 to 5 the criterion allows, so no responsive set can meet the criterion (main reading, arc moves: high 15 to 23, low 7 to 12). With shifted chunks the bounds include the targets in most combinations (arc moves, full trials: high 13 to 21, low 5 to 8), so the claim cannot be decided there without the gaze space. The outcome rests on the permuted reading of the surrogates and does not depend on the move typing.
deviations: The three rotational moves are not named in the paper. Three typings are run: the 36 degree alignment (tags 2xy) and the 72 degree rotations to the right and to the left (tags 3xy, by the sign of the orientation change); the 36 degree alignment right and left and the 72 degree rotation; each transition tag as its own move. High and low are the upper and lower 5% of the surrogates, the level implied by the binomial chance rate of the claims file.
The paper's responsive set cannot be formed (gaze space); the outcome rests on the bounds.
Assumed that the 5 s chunks were permuted (Results, "randomly shuffling periods of spiking activity in time"); under the other reading the outcome is open.

outcomes.statement: A two-way ANOVA of firing on the entry paths by landmark viewed and relative distance gave a main effect of landmark identity in 30 of 111 responsive cells and of relative distance in 64; 29 cells coded a combination (14 with a significant interaction, 15 with both main effects), more than chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Cells encode landmark identity and distance with respect to landmark, paragraph 1; Fig 5
outcomes.quote: A two-way ANOVA revealed a main effect of landmark identity (30 cells out of 111 responsive cells) and relative distance (64 cells out of 111 responsive cells).

statistics.about: cells with a significant interaction (14) or both factors (15)

outcomes.notes: At most 24 cells (over all 186) show a main effect of relative distance with successful laps, and at most 31 with all laps (27 and 33 with type III sums of squares), against 64 +- 6.4; this bound holds for any responsive set. The identity count lies between 15 and 32 (successful laps) or 21 and 47 (all laps) and the interaction count between 5 and 14 or 8 and 17, but the distance count fails under every reading, and with it the partial level. With all laps the one session of 193 trials (sn20110624) gives the residual df of Fig 5, 756, and its three cells have interaction F of 1.83, 3.19 and 1.56, not the 4.41 and 2.12 of Fig 5.
deviations: Laps read two ways, successful trials (Method W) and all trials (Methods, "each of the animal's laps"); the residual df of 756 in Fig 5 is reached only with all laps of sn20110624 (193 x 4 - 16), which supports the second.

Relative distance from the files' curvilinear abscissa in quarters; on the entry paths the abscissa is the distance from the centre over 16 m (0 centre, 1 arm end; median absolute difference at most 0.0023 per file), checked in the notebook; the landmark identity is the entry path. Rates per lap and segment, ANOVA with interaction, type II sums of squares, alpha 0.05; type III, the default of MATLAB's anovan, is shown and gives the same outcome.

outcomes.statement: The main effect of landmark identity was confirmed by a one-way ANOVA on firing to the four landmark views at the center, significant in 12 of 111 responsive cells, more than chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Cells encode landmark identity and distance with respect to landmark, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The main effect of landmark identity was confirmed by a one-way ANOVA on the activity to the four landmark views at the center only (12 cells out of 111 responsive cells, which is a higher proportion than expected by chance; p = 0.01, binomial test).
outcomes.notes: Over the three-space responsive cells and over all cells the one-way count lies between 7 and 16 (reading a) or 10 and 23 (reading b) with successful laps, and between 7 and 18 or 10 and 26 with all laps, so it may or may not fall in 11 to 13, and the binomial test depends on the size of the responsive set, which needs the gaze space.

outcomes.statement: Of 42 cells responding to the appearance of a landmark neighboring the reward, only one was significantly path invariant, while 12 (29%) discriminated significantly between viewpoints of the same landmark; the distribution of indices differed from the surrogates.
outcomes.source: Results, Landmark-triggered activity and viewpoint dependence, paragraph 2; Fig 6D
outcomes.quote: We found that only one landmark-responsive cell was significantly path invariant ( Fig 6B , corresponding to cell 1 in Fig 2 , 5% of the 42 cells, p = 0.37, binomial test), whereas 12/42 cells (29%, p < 0.001, binomial test) discriminated significantly amongst different viewpoints of the same landmark
outcomes.notes: Cells enter on significant point-of-gaze IC, which needs a calibration of the eye signal that the files do not give. Landmark entry into the field of view could be computed from the paper's geometry (landmarks between the arms at twice the arm length, 70 degree field of view) and the camera data, but not on the paper's cell set.

outcomes.statement: Aligned on first foveation of the best-driving landmark, mean activity rose until the saccade to the landmark and peaked shortly after.
outcomes.source: Results, Visual exploration and hippocampal activity dynamics, paragraph 1; Fig 7E
outcomes.quote: Gaze-aligned activity significantly rose until the saccade to the landmark and peaked shortly after.
outcomes.notes: Foveation is gaze within 10 degrees of a landmark, which needs the gaze in degrees; the eye signal has no calibration.

outcomes.statement: Response latencies to the best landmark are left skewed when aligned on gaze and right skewed when aligned on landmark onset, and some cells respond before the landmark enters the field of view.
outcomes.source: Results, Visual exploration and hippocampal activity dynamics, paragraph 1; Fig 7F
outcomes.quote: The distribution of the latencies of the responses to the best landmark are left skewed when aligned on gaze and right skewed when aligned on landmark onset ( Fig 7F , see Materials and Methods ). For a small but nonnegligible proportion of cells, the response latency even preceded the landmark's entry in the FOV
outcomes.notes: Depends on gaze-aligned-dynamics. The gaze-aligned latencies need foveation and the cells are those of gaze-aligned-dynamics; the onset-aligned latencies could be computed from the paper's landmark geometry, but only on another cell set, which would not test the claim.

outcomes.statement: Activity was modulated by the eccentricity of the best-driving landmark, more so just after the landmark appeared, and cells could fire for a landmark not yet visible.
outcomes.source: Results, Visual exploration and hippocampal activity dynamics, paragraph 1; Fig 7G and legend
outcomes.quote: Overall, cells showed a modulation of their activity by landmark eccentricity ( Fig 7G , blue line). This modulation was increased by the recent appearance of the landmark (red line).
outcomes.notes: Depends on gaze-aligned-dynamics; landmark eccentricity relative to gaze needs calibrated gaze.

outcomes.statement: Landmark selectivity was significantly enhanced when the landmark was foveated compared with appearing in the visual periphery, while path selectivity was only moderately improved by direct gaze.
outcomes.source: Results, Visual exploration and hippocampal activity dynamics, paragraph 2; Fig 7H and 7I (the Results cite them as Fig 7G and 7H)
outcomes.quote: Landmark selectivity was significantly enhanced if the landmark was foveated compared to appearing in the visual periphery (one-sided logit-Wilcoxon, p < 0.001, Fig 7G ).
outcomes.notes: Depends on gaze-aligned-dynamics; needs foveation epochs and landmark onsets.

outcomes.statement: Most cells had narrow selectivity and fewer than three positional fields, with an average of 2.7 fields per cell, more than the about 1.5 reported in the rat.
outcomes.source: Results, What is encoded in hippocampal cell activity, paragraph 3; Discussion, Differences and similarities, paragraph 1; S5B Fig
outcomes.quote: In addition, the number of fields per cell (average = 2.7) was greater than the number of fields described in the rat (about 1.5)
outcomes.notes: The paper's text and legends do not define a positional field (S5B counts peaks); the definition is presumably in S1 Appendix, which was not available. The question is for the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: Approximately 50% of the cells showed spatial selectivity like that reported in rats.
outcomes.source: Discussion, Differences and similarities across mammalian hippocampal codes, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Approximately 50% of our cells showed spatial selectivity like that in rats
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a) 0.129 to 0.247 of the 186 cells have significant position IC across the six readings of Method W (46 of 186 under the main one), outside 0.5 +- 0.05. Readings (b) and (c) need the responsive set: responsive cells among all are at least 0.253 to 0.317, and position cells among responsive lie between 0.129 and 0.780, both of which include 0.5. The criterion is met when one reading is within tolerance, so the claim cannot be decided.

outcomes.statement: In the population average of point-of-gaze maps, areas surrounding the landmarks elicited up to 40% more activity than other areas, and all landmarks appeared represented.
outcomes.source: S6C Fig legend; Results, What is encoded in hippocampal cell activity, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Point of gaze map. Areas surrounding the landmarks (black rectangles) elicit up to 40% more activity than other areas.
outcomes.notes: Needs point-of-gaze maps; the eye signal has no calibration.

outcomes.statement: The higher information content of the state space is not due to the higher number of dimensions of that space.
outcomes.source: Results, Sensitivity of the cells, paragraph 3, and Hippocampal cells encode, paragraph 1; S7 Fig
outcomes.quote: This effect cannot be attributed to a modeling bias related to the higher number of dimensions in the state space ( S1 Appendix A5 and S7 Fig ).
outcomes.notes: The control is described in S1 Appendix A5, which was not available; the S7 legend shows only that spikes were simulated on the trajectory with a box-shaped field.

findings.statement: The horizontal and vertical eye signals have no units, calibration or sign convention. They are on a +-5000 scale in 36 hc-12 sessions and a +-5 scale in 26, with saturated samples at the bound (up to 22% of a session). The paper's point-of-gaze maps, foveation and landmark eccentricity cannot be computed, which blocks 11 of the 28 claims and part of a twelfth. The sign used here is inferred from the slow phases during turns.
hc-12 holds 12 probe sessions of monkey K and none of monkey S, where the paper reports 15 and 9; hc-21 holds 8 probe-like sessions, all among K's 12.
87 of the 101 hc-21 files hold the same spike trains (same spike count and first five spike times) as hc-12 files, under other file names. Neither descriptor says that the two data sets overlap.

verifications.reviewed: The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper's full text under paper/. The verifier checked the hc-12 and hc-21 archive listings and scripts for the blocked claims and tested surrogate_counts on synthetic Poisson trains. Its general problems, with what was changed: (2) the shift surrogates overlapped chunks and made a train without coding significant; replaced by rotating each chunk within itself, checked on synthetic trains in the notebook, and every analysis re-run. (3) only the two-sided p was stored; the tails are now kept and the upper tail shown as a variant. (6) the toreward window dropped the returns; a third window, start to reward plus the return, was added, and it is almost the full window as the trial ends at the reward. (10) the camera layout was not checked per file; all 187 files have 12 columns, tags 101 to 555, radius 0.81 to 3.0, and entry headings on the 72 degree grid, which explains the orientation range of ke20140207; the abscissa of 1.618 in sn20110610 falls on no entry path.

disagreements.reason: Cell 26: the eye signal differs between right and left returns in each monkey, p <= 1.5e-10 under every reading. The side relative to the turn is not tested independently, because the sign was chosen on the assumption that the eyes deviate toward the side the view rotates to, and that is what this test measures (problem 1).

Cell 32, permute surrogates, cell set (b): IC higher in the centre at p = 0.045 and sparsity higher at p = 0.0074. Neither reaches p < 0.001. Set (b) here is the three-space responsive set, standing in for the four-space set.
Cell 34: the closest reading, (b) with permute, tests n = 59 cells (tolerance met), 4 high (band met), but 16 low against 20 +- 2. Every other reading also misses the low count.

Cell 47 (full/permute): state minus position, median 0.014, p = 1.1e-4; state minus direction, median 0.021, p = 2.5e-7. These are two of the three comparisons, which the criterion grades as partial. The notebook marks the claim blocked although these two comparisons need no gaze (problem 5); they are also shown only for full/permute.

verifications.reviewed: The full executed notebook of the first revision, the helper module, the claims file and the attempt record, with the paper under paper/. It found round-1 problems 1 to 10 resolved, and reported text that did not match the outputs, with what was changed: cell 9 said that at the trial start the abscissa is at the arm end and that one second after the arrival at the centre it is not 0, which the printed values contradict; cell 7 and the landmark-identity-distance deviation said the abscissa runs from 0 at the centre to 1 at the arm end, where the outputs also fit an abscissa that runs from the start of each branch. The notebook now prints the abscissa against the distance from the centre over 16 m: on the entry and exit paths they agree in every file (median absolute difference at most 0.0023), so 0 is the centre there; at the trial start the row still belongs to the passive return, whose abscissa has run down to 0.01 while the camera is at the arm end (1.00); after the arrival the camera stays at the centre while the view rotates. Cells 7 and 9 and the deviation were rewritten to match. The README row of state-space-selectivity now carries the permuted-chunk qualifier, and the record's statement that the low count of direction-tuning-not-maintained misses under every reading now says it holds over the stand-in sets only.

paper_notes.statement: How were the 5 s chunks of recording "randomly shifted" for the surrogates (their order permuted, or each shifted by its own offset), and did the maps include the passive returns after successful trials? Significant counts change between these readings (state space 57 or 47 of 186 cells with returns, 42 or 37 without), sparsity-state-vs-direction holds only with the returns, and state-space-selectivity is decided only with permuted chunks.
Which learning-curve method is reference 60, and how were trials to criterion counted after the new entries of probe sessions? The files hold only whole-session curves.

How is a positional field defined for the count of 2.7 fields per cell, and how was the control for the dimensionality of the state space done (S1 Appendix A5)? S1 Appendix was not available to this attempt.

Which three rotational moves enter the state-space selectivity index, and were the two-way ANOVA's laps all trials or only successful ones? The residual df of 756 in Fig 5 fits all 193 laps of session sn20110624.

entries.name: wirth-2017
entries.title: Space in the macaque hippocampus during virtual navigation (Wirth et al. 2017)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Wirth, Baraduc, Plante, Pinede and Duhamel (2017) on CRCNS hc-12, which holds 189 hippocampal cells of two macaques navigating a virtual star maze with eye tracking, and uses CRCNS hc-21 to check which of its recordings are also in hc-12. It covers learning, gaze before turns and on passive returns, information content in position, direction and state space, centre and return direction maps, state-space selectivity and the landmark ANOVAs. The point-of-gaze analyses need a calibration of the eye signal that the files do not give.
